strengths: The paper addresses an important practical combination—temporally synchronized video-to-audio generation, few-step sampling, audio conditioning, and long-form extension—in one coherent system. The reported gains are potentially significant for Foley and sound-design workflows.

The method combines shortcut flow matching, masked audio conditioning/outpainting, and a high-temporal-resolution audiovisual encoder in a technically plausible architecture. Applying shortcut models to video-to-audio generation appears original, even though the individual ingredients are largely established.

Evaluation covers several relevant dimensions: distributional audio metrics, semantic and temporal alignment, a blind listening study, sampling-step scaling, generation length, audio conditioning, and model-size/objective ablations. Table 1 reports particularly strong synchronization results: DeSync improves from 0.521 for MMAudio to 0.497, while human synchronization MOS improves from 2.92 to 3.52.

The shortcut results are promising: Figure 5 indicates little degradation at eight sampling steps, while Table 2 suggests shortcut training does not materially reduce 32-step performance relative to ordinary flow matching.

The manuscript is generally well organized, gives useful architectural and training details, includes limitations concerning scene changes in progressive outpainting, and presents readable figures and tables. weaknesses: The evidence does not fully support two central claims. “Near-real-time” generation is asserted without wall-clock latency, real-time factor, memory use, hardware-specific throughput, or an inference-cost comparison. “Unconstrained-length” generation is evaluated only up to 60 seconds and only through FAD and DeSync; there is no measurement or listening study for boundary artifacts, error accumulation, long-range consistency, or repeated outpainting over substantially longer sequences.

The long-form comparison is narrow and insufficiently controlled. Only MMAudio is shown in Figure 5, despite the discussion of LoVA and V-AURA, and SALSA-V uses iterative 9.5-second extension while MMAudio processes the whole sequence. This compares different inference strategies without stitching or sliding-window baselines. Moreover, the main test set is described as containing videos up to 30 seconds, whereas Figure 5 reports 60-second evaluation; the size, origin, and construction of this dedicated long-form set are not specified.

Key experimental details are missing. The test-set sample count, source proportions, deduplication procedures, exact filtering threshold, uncertainty across samples or seeds, and statistical significance are absent. Most improvements in Tables 1–2 are small and reported without confidence intervals. The custom synchronization representation is not directly ablated against SynchFormer features, and the paper provides no ablation isolating masked training or the claimed batch-size effect.

The human study is underreported: it uses only 18 participants and 10 hand-selected videos, with no confidence intervals or hypothesis tests. “Qualified” is undefined, and recruitment, screening, listening equipment/environment, compensation, participant demographics, and ethics/consent procedures are omitted. The statement that the study yielded 180 individual scores is also ambiguous because each trial contains three systems and three rating axes.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale and novelty of the work. The samples link is blank (“Samples are available at.”), no code, checkpoints, or release commitment is provided, and portions of the training data and evaluation set are private or vaguely described. Training requires multiple one-million-step stages and a proprietary studio Foley dataset, but total compute, training time, preprocessing details, dataset splits, and model initialization/checkpoint identifiers are not fully documented.

The shortcut objective is not specified sufficiently to reproduce. Equation 2 leaves the construction of v_target undefined, does not describe stop-gradient handling or the distribution and discretization of d and t, and appears to sum flow-matching and self-consistency terms although the text says only a fraction of each batch receives consistency targets. The sampling integrator and step schedule are also omitted.

The audio-conditioning evaluation is weak and potentially biased. Figure 6 uses an unspecified “representative subset” selected to contain recurring characteristic sounds, reports no sample size or baseline, and tests continuation from ground-truth audio rather than transfer from an independent reference. Thus it does not establish the broader claim that users can control spectral characteristics for professional sound design.

The proposed SWSD metric has a technical problem as written: log-mel entries can be negative, so normalizing each vector by its sum does not generally produce a probability mass function. The metric is also introduced without validation against perceptual judgments or established style/spectral-similarity measures. The description of a “per-sample FAD” likewise needs a precise definition because standard FAD is a distribution-level statistic.

There are smaller internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: the mask range is stated as starting at 5 ms although one token at the reported 43 Hz latent rate is about 23 ms; several results are available only as plots rather than numerical tables; and the manuscript sometimes conflates “overall fit” with audio quality even though SALSA-V's audio-quality MOS (2.96) is below MMAudio's (3.16).

The ethics and data-governance discussion is incomplete. Training uses in-the-wild YouTube-derived material and a private dataset without discussing licenses, consent, privacy, copyrighted audio, or release constraints. Potential misuse of synchronized synthetic audio and the ethical oversight of the listener study are also unaddressed. Overall, the idea and preliminary results have clear merit, but these evidential and reproducibility gaps prevent reliable validation of the paper's strongest claims.

strengths: Originality/significance: Combining shortcut flow matching, masked audio conditioning/outpainting, and high-frame-rate audiovisual features is a practically motivated contribution. Applying shortcut models to video-to-audio generation appears novel, even though the individual ingredients are adapted from prior work.

Soundness: On the authors' test set, SALSA-V is competitive with MMAudio across several standard metrics and obtains better reported FAD, ImageBind similarity, DeSync, overall-fit MOS, and synchronization MOS, despite having fewer parameters.

The model-size/objective ablation suggests that adding shortcut training does not noticeably degrade 32-step generation. Figure 5 also provides promising evidence that the resulting model is robust at low sampling-step budgets.

Presentation: The architecture, training stages, conditioning sources, and main implementation hyperparameters are generally described clearly. The paper also candidly acknowledges lower subjective audio quality than MMAudio and the failure of progressive outpainting across scene changes.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not isolate the paper's central components. Shortcut and ordinary flow-matching models are compared only at 32 steps; the crucial low-step comparison is instead against MMAudio, so the few-step advantage cannot be attributed specifically to the shortcut objective. Likewise, there is no ablation replacing the proposed synchronization encoder with SynchFormer features, and no controlled ablation of masked training.

The baseline selection is inadequate for the main claims. Long-form evaluation compares only with MMAudio while omitting explicitly relevant long-form methods such as LoVA and V-AURA. Efficient sampling is not compared with Frieren, despite discussing it as the pertinent efficient V2A baseline. General results include only two baselines.

The evaluation set is not reproducibly specified: its size, exact mixture of sources, sampling procedure, deduplication, captions, and release status are absent. It combines a holdout set of unspecified in-the-wild videos with public sets, making both leakage risk and statistical reliability impossible to assess. No uncertainty or significance testing is given for Table 1.

The human study is too small and underreported to support broad superiority claims: only 10 deliberately selected videos and 18 participants are used, with no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, participant-selection criteria beyond 'qualified,' or repeated-measures analysis. The manuscript calls 180 trials 'individual scores,' although each trial contains ratings for three systems on three axes. SALSA-V also loses to MMAudio on the actual audio-quality MOS (2.96 versus 3.16), contrary to the abstract's broad claim of outperforming prior methods in the listening study.

The audio-conditioning evidence is weak. It uses an undefined 'representative subset,' has no competing conditioning baseline or human evaluation, and changes the length of the evaluated suffix as the prepend duration grows. The proposed SWSD normalization divides log-mel values by their signed sum while claiming to create a probability mass function; log-mel entries need not be nonnegative, so this construction is not mathematically justified as stated. 'Per-sample FAD' is also nonstandard and insufficiently defined.

The long-form comparison is confounded: SALSA-V generates successive 9.5-second chunks with a 0.5-second carryover, whereas MMAudio processes the full sequence. There is no evaluation of boundary artifacts, cumulative drift, semantic consistency, or listener preference on long clips. Testing only up to 60 seconds does not substantiate 'unconstrained length,' particularly given the admitted failure on scene cuts.

The near-real-time claim is unsupported because the paper reports neither wall-clock latency, real-time factor, throughput, hardware-specific inference measurements, nor the cost of repeatedly encoding overlapping long-form windows. Eight sampling steps alone do not establish near-real-time operation.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The samples link is blank, no code or checkpoints are provided, and important data are vaguely described as an in-the-wild Panda70M/YouTube collection and a high-fidelity studio Foley set. Filtering thresholds, retained sample counts by source, preprocessing, full shortcut-target construction, evaluation sample counts, and random seeds are missing.

Research ethics and data governance are not addressed. The manuscript gives no information about licenses or consent for collected YouTube and proprietary Foley material, participant consent/compensation or study approval, or risks arising from generated audio being mistaken for authentic recorded events. These omissions are material for a model trained on web audiovisual content.

Presentation contains several overclaims and inconsistencies: 'significantly outperforms' is used without statistical testing; 'overall quality' is sometimes conflated with the separate overall-fit and audio-quality study axes; Equation 2 does not reflect the stated 25% mixture cleanly and leaves the self-consistency target insufficiently defined; and multiple results are conveyed only by small plots without exact numerical tables. Overall, the ideas are promising, but the missing controlled comparisons and under-specified evaluation prevent the central claims from being considered reliable or reproducible.

strengths: Soundness: The method is technically coherent, combining a dedicated 24-FPS audiovisual synchronization encoder, masked flow matching for audio conditioning and outpainting, and shortcut training for few-step inference. The component comparison in Table 2 indicates that shortcut training preserves 32-step performance relative to standard flow matching.

Evaluation: SALSA-V is competitive with or better than the evaluated baselines across several metrics. It improves FAD from 1.12 to 1.07 and DeSync from 0.521 to 0.497 over MMAudio, while the human study reports a notably higher synchronization score of 3.52 versus 2.92. Figure 5 also shows substantially better robustness when reducing the sampling budget.

Significance: Few-step, synchronized, audio-conditioned, and extensible video-to-audio generation is practically useful for Foley and sound-design workflows. Maintaining quality at eight sampling steps and extending generation to 60 seconds are meaningful capabilities if reproduced.

Originality: The individual ingredients are largely adapted from prior work, but their integration is novel for video-to-audio generation. In particular, applying shortcut models to generative audio and combining them with masked outpainting and higher-resolution synchronization features constitutes a useful contribution.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with an informative architecture diagram, qualitative spectrograms, ablations, implementation details, and an honest discussion of the audio-quality gap and scene-cut limitation.
weaknesses: Soundness and evidential scope: The strongest claims are insufficiently established. No wall-clock latency, real-time factor, memory usage, or hardware-specific inference measurement is reported, so eight sampling steps do not by themselves justify the repeated near-real-time claim. Likewise, evaluation only to 60 seconds does not establish unconstrained-length generation.

Long-form evaluation is incomplete: The comparison uses only MMAudio and omits the explicitly long-form LoVA baseline and the autoregressive V-AURA approach discussed in related work. FAD and DeSync do not measure boundary artifacts, temporal continuity, or long-range coherence, and there is no human study of long-form outputs. Progressive outpainting also uses only 0.5 seconds of retained context and is acknowledged to fail across scene changes.

Statistical rigor: The manuscript does not report the size or precise composition of its custom test set, uncertainty over objective metrics, or significance tests. The human study contains only 18 participants and 10 selected videos, with no confidence intervals or analysis accounting for repeated ratings. Consequently, small differences such as DeSync 0.521 versus 0.497 and overall fit 3.43 versus 3.29 are difficult to interpret.

Audio-conditioning evidence is limited to a selected, unspecified-size subset containing repeated characteristic sounds. The proposed SWSD metric is newly introduced without validation against human judgments, and the algorithm is stochastic but provides no sensitivity analysis. Calling log-mel vectors probability mass functions after L1 normalization is also questionable because log-mel entries can be negative.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the work. The paper provides useful optimizer and training summaries, but omits important architectural hyperparameters, the shortcut step-size distribution and complete target construction, data-filtering thresholds, evaluation-set identifiers, and the size of conditioning subsets. The samples URL is blank, no code or checkpoints are provided, and parts of the training data are an unspecified in-the-wild YouTube collection and proprietary studio Foley set.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: masking for in/outpainting, pretrained synchronization representations, flow matching, and shortcut objectives all originate in prior work. The paper demonstrates an effective combination but offers limited new analysis of why these components interact successfully.

Ethics and limitations treatment is incomplete. The technical limitations discussion is candid, but the paper does not address licensing or consent for collected YouTube and studio data, possible memorization, copyright implications, or misuse of generated audio. These concerns are especially relevant for a media-generation system.

strengths: The paper addresses practically important limitations of video-to-audio systems—temporal synchronization, long-form generation, reference-audio conditioning, and sampling cost—in one coherent system.

The combination of masked flow matching with shortcut training is useful and appears technically plausible. Results indicate that the shortcut objective preserves 32-step performance while remaining effective at 4–8 steps, without a separate distillation stage.

Evaluation covers several complementary dimensions, including FAD, two KL metrics, Inception Score, ImageBind similarity, SynchFormer-based desynchronization, runtime, and a blinded listening study. SALSA-V achieves especially strong synchronization results: DeSync improves from 0.521 for MMAudio to 0.497, while subjective synchronization improves from 2.92 to 3.52.

The few-step and duration sweeps are valuable. Unlike MMAudio, SALSA-V degrades only modestly as the sampling budget decreases or duration increases; the 4-step comparison with Frieren also favors SALSA-V across every reported metric.

The authors acknowledge an important long-form limitation: progressive outpainting may incorrectly carry acoustic characteristics across scene cuts. The impact statement also recognizes plausible media-manipulation risks.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually polished, with helpful architectural diagrams, spectrograms, algorithmic description, and substantial implementation detail.
weaknesses: The evaluation set is insufficiently specified. Its total size, composition by source and duration, sampling procedure, prompts, preprocessing, and overlap checks against the large YouTube-derived training collection are not reported. Consequently, the broad quantitative comparisons cannot be independently interpreted or reproduced, and possible train–test leakage is not ruled out.

No confidence intervals, repeated-generation variability, or significance tests are reported for any automatic result. Many claimed gains are small—for example DeSync 0.497 versus 0.521 and overall MOS 3.43 versus 3.29—so it is unclear whether they are statistically meaningful.

The human study is underpowered and incompletely documented: only 18 participants and 10 selected videos are used, participant qualification is undefined, and no uncertainty, inter-rater agreement, significance analysis, compensation, consent, or ethics-review information is given. The statement that the study produced 180 individual scores is also inconsistent with rating three tracks on three axes unless “score” means a trial rather than an individual rating.

The central synchronization contribution is not isolated experimentally. The new VideoPrism/AST alignment model is neither directly benchmarked against SynchFormer nor ablated within the generator. There are likewise no component ablations for synchronization features, semantic features, masking, overlap length, or audio-conditioning guidance, making it difficult to attribute the gains.

The evidence does not fully support the claimed “seamless” and long-range generation. Long-form output is produced by repeatedly generating 9.5 seconds from only 0.5 seconds of prior audio; there is no boundary-artifact metric, listening study on long clips, comparison with ordinary overlap-and-stitch baselines, or test of consistency beyond local spectral carryover. Table 5 contains only one long-form baseline and no uncertainty.

The audio-conditioning experiment uses an unspecified “representative subset” deliberately selected to contain recurring characteristic sounds. Its sample count and selection protocol are absent, inviting selection bias. Moreover, “per-sample FAD” is not adequately defined, since standard FAD is a distribution-level statistic.

The proposed SWSD description is mathematically confused: log-mel entries can be negative, so column-wise L1 normalization does not make them probability mass functions as claimed. The algorithm subsequently treats time frames as empirical samples and computes sliced Wasserstein distances, for which that probability-mass interpretation is unnecessary. This weakens confidence in the new metric and its conditioning conclusions.

Reproducibility is limited despite useful optimizer and architecture details. The project-page field is blank; no code, checkpoints, evaluation lists, random seeds, exact filtering thresholds, data-source proportions, or compute totals are provided. A proprietary studio Foley dataset and private holdout videos are used, further preventing reconstruction of training and evaluation.

The shortcut formulation is underspecified: the units and distribution of step size d, valid relationships between t and d, loss weighting, and construction of the stated 25% consistency subset are not fully defined, while the displayed objective appears to add both losses for every sample. These ambiguities impede faithful implementation.

Originality is primarily in integrating established masked conditioning, pretrained audiovisual encoders, and shortcut-model training into video-to-audio generation. This is a useful engineering contribution, but the paper provides limited new analysis or methodological insight beyond demonstrating the combination.

The ethics discussion identifies deceptive-media risk but provides no concrete provenance, watermarking, misuse evaluation, or release safeguards. It also omits licensing, privacy, and consent considerations for the in-the-wild YouTube-derived data.

strengths: The paper targets a useful combination of capabilities—temporally aligned video-to-audio generation, reference-audio conditioning, long-form extension, and few-step inference—and presents a coherent architecture combining masked flow matching with shortcut training.

The shortcut result is promising: Table 2 compares otherwise matched flow-matching and shortcut variants and suggests that shortcut training preserves 32-step performance, while Table 3 reports substantial four-step gains over Frieren.

The evaluation covers several relevant dimensions, including distributional metrics, semantic and temporal alignment, runtime, model scaling, conditioning, and a listening study. SALSA-V reports particularly strong DeSync and human synchronization scores.

The manuscript is generally clear and polished, provides useful training and architectural details in the appendix, and honestly acknowledges that progressive outpainting can improperly carry acoustic characteristics across scene cuts.
The impact statement recognizes media-manipulation risks rather than presenting the technology as ethically neutral.
weaknesses: The central synchronization contribution is not adequately isolated or validated. The new contrastive synchronization encoder is never evaluated directly on synchronization or retrieval benchmarks, and there is no ablation replacing it with SynchFormer or removing its conditioning. Consequently, the reported end-to-end gains cannot be attributed to the claimed high-resolution synchronization representation.

The quantitative evaluation is insufficiently specified for verification. The manuscript does not report the objective test-set size, source proportions, construction of the private holdout set, number of generations or seeds, or confidence intervals. Most improvements over MMAudio in Table 1 are small—for example, DeSync changes from 0.521 to 0.497 and FAD from 1.12 to 1.07—so uncertainty is essential.

The listening study is too limited to substantiate the broad human-preference claims: it uses only 10 deliberately selected videos and 18 vaguely described “qualified” participants, provides no confidence intervals or significance tests, and omits recruitment, compensation, exclusion, and consent details. The accounting of “180 individual scores” is also unclear because every trial rates three systems on three axes. Moreover, SALSA-V's reported audio-quality MOS is lower than MMAudio's, 2.96 versus 3.16, weakening the high-fidelity claim.

The claimed “unconstrained,” “seamless” long-form generation is not demonstrated. Evaluation stops at 60 seconds, the LoVA comparison stops at 30 seconds, and there is no listening test or boundary-specific artifact metric for the repeated 0.5-second-context stitching procedure. Accumulated drift over genuinely long sequences is untested, while the admitted failure on scene cuts further narrows the claim.

The audio-conditioning evidence is weak. Figure 6 uses an unspecified “representative subset,” reports no sample count, uncertainty, or competing conditioning baseline, and introduces SWSD without validation against perception. Calling normalized log-mel values probability masses is mathematically questionable because log-mel entries need not be nonnegative, and “per-sample FAD” is not a standard use of a distributional Fréchet metric.

Baseline fairness and experimental controls are unclear. The custom mixed-duration test set is unavailable, baseline checkpoints and inference settings are not enumerated beyond “author-recommended,” and comparisons confound architecture, parameter count, training data, codec, and conditioning model. The few-step MMAudio curve appears to reduce its solver steps without an efficiency-specific adaptation, while the most favorable direct optimized comparison is only against Frieren at one four-step setting.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The project-page field is blank; no code, checkpoints, prompts, evaluation examples, or listener materials are supplied. Key ingredients are private or underspecified, including the in-the-wild YouTube collection, studio Foley data, filtering threshold, test split, VAE losses, and complete transformer configuration. Reproducing the reported results would therefore be impractical.

The ethics discussion is incomplete for the data and study used. It does not address licensing, creator consent, privacy, or potentially sensitive content in scraped YouTube/Panda70M material, nor governance of the proprietary Foley set. It also gives no human-subjects protocol information and offers only a generic statement that deployment safeguards “may be necessary.”

Overall, the ideas are promising and the reported numbers merit further investigation, but unsupported central claims, missing statistical evidence, inadequate attribution ablations, and poor reproducibility prevent reliable acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Soundness: The core empirical picture is promising. SALSA-V achieves the best reported FAD-VGG, ImageBind alignment, and DeSync results in Table 1, while Table 3 shows a substantial advantage over the distilled Frieren model at four sampling steps. Using SynchFormer rather than the authors' own alignment model for synchronization evaluation reduces concern about a self-evaluation bias.

The experiments address several practically relevant capabilities: standard video-to-audio generation, few-step sampling, 30-60-second generation, audio-conditioned continuation, runtime, model scaling, and human judgments. The shortcut-versus-standard-flow comparison also indicates that shortcut training does not materially degrade 32-step performance.

Significance: Combining fast sampling, temporal synchronization, reference-audio conditioning, and iterative long-form extension in one 643M-parameter system would be useful for Foley and sound-design workflows. Generating 10 seconds of audio in 0.71 seconds at four steps on an A100 is practically meaningful, although the paper's near-real-time wording understates this faster-than-real-time result.

Originality: The individual ingredients largely build on prior shortcut models, masked generation, pretrained audiovisual encoders, and multimodal diffusion transformers, but their integration for video-to-audio is novel and produces a capable system. The dedicated high-temporal-resolution VideoPrism/AST synchronization representation is also a sensible contribution.

Presentation is generally polished and easy to follow, with clear architectural diagrams, readable spectrogram examples, detailed optimization settings, and an honest discussion of the principal failure mode of iterative continuation across scene cuts. The manuscript also acknowledges media-manipulation risks rather than hiding them. weaknesses: Soundness: The evaluation protocol is underspecified. The paper does not report the number or composition of examples used for the main objective evaluation, the duration-scaling curves, or the 'representative subset' used for audio conditioning. Error bars appear in figures without an explanation, and tables lack confidence intervals or statistical tests. Consequently, small advantages such as DeSync 0.497 versus 0.521 and MOS 3.43 versus 3.29 cannot be judged statistically reliable.

The human study is too small and incompletely reported for strong perceptual claims: it uses only 18 participants and 10 hand-selected videos, gives no uncertainty or significance analysis, and does not describe recruitment, demographics, compensation, consent, or ethics review. Moreover, the main text describes the 3.43 column as 'overall quality,' while the appendix defines it as semantic 'Overall Fit'; SALSA-V actually trails MMAudio on the separate audio-quality score, 2.96 versus 3.16.

The strongest long-form language is not fully supported. Evaluation only reaches 60 seconds, the direct LoVA comparison is at 30 seconds, and there is no listening study or boundary-specific metric for stitching artifacts. Distributional and synchronization metrics may miss perceptible discontinuities or gradual semantic drift, so claims of 'seamless' and unconstrained-length synthesis should be moderated.

Important ablations are missing. There is no controlled ablation of the proposed synchronization encoder against SynchFormer or simpler pretrained features, no masked-objective ablation for long-form generation, and no comparison between iterative continuation and processing the same duration directly with SALSA-V. Thus, the evidence does not isolate which proposed component causes the synchronization and long-form gains.

Reproducibility is limited despite useful training hyperparameters. The project-page field is blank, and no code, checkpoints, evaluation list, prompts, seeds, preprocessing thresholds, precise architecture dimensions, or complete dataset mixture is provided. The proprietary high-fidelity Foley data and vaguely specified in-the-wild YouTube collection further prevent independent reconstruction. It is also unclear whether strict splits were used when VGGSound trained the generator and synchronization encoder while its test set contributed to evaluation.

Several technical details need correction or clarification: Equation 2 depicts flow-matching and self-consistency losses as simultaneously summed although the text says different batch subsets receive different targets; the units/range of shortcut step size d and handling of t+d are unclear; the stated 5 ms minimum mask conflicts with the appendix's one-token minimum at 43 Hz; and the exact clamping procedure during masked integration is omitted.

The limitations and ethics discussion is directionally appropriate but narrow. It does not address dataset licensing and consent for scraped YouTube or studio audio, possible reproduction of voices or copyrighted sounds through reference conditioning, demographic or content biases, or concrete provenance/watermarking and misuse mitigations. These concerns are material for releasing a realistic media-generation system.
